alt: The ten retailer types in their usual grouping. Small-scale: itinerant retailer, vending machine, independent retailer, street market and speciality shop. Large-scale: online retailer, multiple chain store, supermarket, hypermarket and department store, each with its main feature.
caption: Learn one identifying feature for each type; judge an online retailer’s scale from the case.

alt: Three columns compare a supermarket (self-service, mainly food), a hypermarket (very large, out of town, food and non-food, car parks) and a department store (city centre, many departments), each with one advantage and one disadvantage.
caption: Use the distinguishing features, not just size, to tell the large stores apart.

after: ## Why the small-scale retailer often survives
alt: A small retailer survives through the three syllabus examples: personal service, flexible opening hours and additional services. Further reasons are a location close to homes, selling small quantities and joining a voluntary chain.
caption: Small shops survive by offering what large retailers find hard to copy.

alt: The eleven selling techniques grouped by how they raise sales: recognition (branding, logos, packaging), price and cost (own brands, self service), loyalty (loyalty programmes, direct mail, informal credit), confidence (after-sales service, cash on delivery) and speed (barcoding).
caption: Explain a technique by saying how it raises sales or loyalty for the shop described.

alt: Left: multi-channel retailing sells through a shop, website and app that may run separately. Right: omnichannel retailing links the channels to one account, the same prices, stock information and loyalty points, so a customer can start on the app and finish in the shop.
caption: Omnichannel joins the channels into one experience; multi-channel channels may run separately.

alt: A barcode on the product is scanned at an EPoS till, a computerised till that records each sale and updates stock records.
caption: Do not confuse the barcode on the product with the EPoS till that reads it.

after: ## Effects of ecommerce on traditional commerce
alt: Five positive impacts of ecommerce on traditional commerce, such as 24/7 selling and more customers, beside four negative impacts, such as delivery and website maintenance costs. A bookshop adding a website reaches readers nationwide but pays for packaging, couriers and site upkeep.
caption: The overall effect depends on the product and the customers, so weigh both sides.

alt: Four steps of the answer for a family clothing shop losing customers to a hypermarket: name a loyalty programme, explain how points work, link it to keeping customers from the hypermarket, and justify it with personal offers a hypermarket is unlikely to make.
caption: Name, explain, link to the problem, then justify for this shop.
